rationale: A wins because it keeps the story bounded to what the update can actually support, then names the missing proof instead of decorating around it. Its strongest line, "Glossier's wholesale channel is now growing faster than the DTC business it was built on," is a real retail-strategy pitch with an editor-shaped tension. B has instincts, but "Glossier times its first fragrance launch to its biggest retail push yet" invents timing strategy, says "first fragrance launch" when the update says first fragrance line extension, and turns a usable fact into a correction risk.
gaps_in_A: "A retail reporter covering Sephora and LVMH's specialty-retail strategy" imports LVMH context that was not in the supplied update. Common knowledge is still not supplied evidence.
"suburban strip-mall retail rather than mall-and-city Sephora" overreads Sephora at Kohl's. The update gives the channel, not the shopper geography or store-format thesis.

A mostly refuses fragrance. That is right for a generic product-listing angle, but it misses a conditional angle connecting fragrance sampling to expanded physical distribution if Glossier can prove that link.
gaps_in_B: "Glossier times its first fragrance launch to its biggest retail push yet" is the worst offender: the update says first fragrance line extension, not first fragrance launch, and "times" asserts strategy the facts do not prove.
"Sephora at Kohl's becomes a test case for prestige beauty in a big-box mall" piles on unsupported framing: "test case," "prestige," and "big-box mall" are not in the update.
"Glossier's whole mythology was direct-only" turns a channel history into brand mythology without evidence. It is plausible, but plausible is where lazy pitches go to sound smart.
"mid-market and suburban shoppers" and "coastal-urban" invent a customer-access geography the update does not supply. Good reporter shape, bad factual footing.
